title: An Interview with Nora Bennett
subject: Nora Bennett
text:
TITLE: An Interview with Nora Bennett
SUBJECT: Nora Bennett, sometimes called Norrie by her sisters and Nor by her grandchildren
INTERVIEWER: Helen Ward
DATE OF INTERVIEW: 2026-02-14
NOTE: This is fictional training data for the Memoirs demo. All names, places and events are invented.

[00:00:12] HELEN: To begin, where did you grow up?

[00:00:18] NORA: In Liverpool, mostly. I was born in the spring of 1949, although my mother always said it was the last cold week of March and my birth certificate says April 2. We lived in a narrow brick house near the old docks. My dad worked there for a while, loading timber, and later repaired lifts in warehouses. Mum took in alterations. She could turn a curtain into a school uniform if you gave her an afternoon.

[00:01:31] NORA: There were four of us girls, though people sometimes think there were three because my youngest sister June was born quite a bit later. I was the eldest, so I was Norrie at home. I stopped using that name when I left England. In Australia I became Nora, and then my grandchildren decided I was Nana Norrie again.

[00:02:08] HELEN: What did you want to do as a child?

[00:02:15] NORA: I wanted to work in a library. That sounds very quiet, but the library was where I learned that the world was much larger than our street. I left school at sixteen and worked in a dress shop first. In 1968 I started part-time at the municipal library in Toxteth. I was not a librarian in the grand sense. I stamped cards, repaired books and helped children find things about dinosaurs.

[00:03:22] NORA: I met Alan at a dance in 1969. He was playing bass in a band that knew six songs and played all of them twice. We married in September 1970 at St Luke's. Alan's full name was Alan Bennett, but almost everybody called him Al. He was a refrigeration mechanic, which became important later because that was the reason we ended up leaving England.

[00:04:17] NORA: Our daughter Priya was born in 1978. I say 1978 because that is how I remember it, but Priya keeps telling me the hospital record says January 1979. She arrived just after midnight, so perhaps we can both be right emotionally. Our son Daniel came along in 1981. He was a very serious baby and is now a man who sends jokes by text.

[00:05:04] HELEN: How did you come to Australia?

[00:05:11] NORA: Alan was offered work maintaining cold-storage equipment in Adelaide. We talked about it for nearly a year. We flew out near the end of 1986, or it may have been February 1987. I remember Priya being upset because she had to leave her teacher, Mrs Evans. The first house was in Woodville, with a lemon tree that produced fruit the size of tennis balls.

[00:06:03] NORA: I missed the rain for about two weeks and then stopped missing it. Adelaide was dry and bright. We had no family there, which was frightening, but people were kind. Alan worked long hours. I did cleaning, then found work at a school library. I never stopped wanting to be around books.

[00:07:14] HELEN: Tell me about Mei.

[00:07:19] NORA: Mei Tan. Her surname was Chen before she married, though she has always used Tan professionally. I met her at an evening English class, probably in 1988. She sat next to me and corrected my pronunciation of "schedule". We became friends because neither of us wanted to go home straight after class. She had lived in Adelaide since the seventies and knew where to buy decent rice and where not to park on a Saturday.

[00:08:13] NORA: In the early nineties we opened a small cafe called The Lantern on Grange Road. Mei says we opened in 1992. I say 1991 because I remember the recession being discussed on the radio and I associate the opening with that winter. The lease says Mei is probably right. It was not a fashionable place. We served soup, toasties, tea and a cake that Priya still claims was too dry.

[00:09:20] NORA: The cafe survived because people came back. A nurse from the hospital brought her night-shift colleagues. Students sat there for hours over one cup of coffee. Mei handled the kitchen and suppliers. I handled the books, the notices and the customers who wanted to tell us their whole family history while we were trying to close.

[00:10:12] NORA: We closed The Lantern in 2003. Alan's health was beginning to fail and Mei wanted to spend more time with her mother. It was sad, but not a disaster. I went back to the school library, and in 2005 I started a local oral-history group. That is probably when I finally became what I wanted to be at sixteen, someone who helped people find and keep their stories.

[00:11:19] HELEN: What would you want your family to remember?

[00:11:27] NORA: That an ordinary life is not a small life. My mother altered clothes for forty years and could remember every person who had sat at her table. Alan repaired machines nobody noticed until they stopped working. Mei and I served soup in a little cafe. None of that sounds grand, but it held people together. That is the part I want kept.
